# CHESS.EXE reverse engineering

*README.MD file mostly generated by Anthropic's Claude AI because Thomas Dzubin hates documenting code.  LOL*

Reverse-engineering `CHESS.EXE`, an 8086 MS-DOS program from the 1980s, with
the goal of rewriting it as portable, hardware-independent C so it can be
understood, modified, and recompiled. Identified from embedded strings as
**CHESS88 V2.0 — A CHESS PROGRAM FOR THE IBM PERSONAL COMPUTER BY DON BERG**.

## Folders

- `original/` — the untouched original `CHESS.EXE`, plus a raw extracted
  load module (`CHESS_loadmodule.bin`, header stripped, no relocation
  applied — for quick byte-level poking, not authoritative).
- `disasm/` — generated disassembly (`chess_disasm.txt`) and Ghidra
  decompiler pseudocode (`chess_decompiled.c`) for all 38 functions Ghidra
  found. Regenerated from `ghidra_project/` — see `notes/analysis.md` for
  the exact commands.
- `ghidra_project/` — the Ghidra project database (`ChessProject`). Open
  this in the Ghidra GUI to browse/annotate interactively instead of
  reading the flat text exports.
- `notes/` — working analysis notes (`analysis.md`), the MZ-header parser
  script and its output (`parse_mz.py`, `header.txt`), the strings dump
  script and output (`strings.py`, `strings.txt`), and the Ghidra export
  script (`ghidra_scripts/ExportChess.java`).
- `src/` — the C rewrite: a working, playable chess engine, buildable
  either as a plain-text console game or with a graphical board.
  `chess.h` holds every constant (board layout, piece codes, evaluation
  weights); `board.c`/`movegen.c` are the portable core (board setup, move
  generation, make/unmake, check detection); `eval.c`/`search.c` are the
  evaluator and iterative-deepening alpha-beta search; `display.h` is the
  thin, swappable platform layer, with two interchangeable backends:
  `display_console.c` (plain stdio, letters) and `display_graphics.c`
  (draws the board via `board_render.c`). `main.c` ties it together and is
  shared by both. Build both with CMake:

      cd src
      cmake -B build -G Ninja
      cmake --build build
      ./build/chess-Windows.exe        # text board, any terminal (chess-Linux on Linux)
      ./build/chess_gfx-Windows.exe    # graphical board, writes chess_board.ppm

  ### Graphics

  The piece artwork is the *original's own* pixel data, extracted
  byte-for-byte from `CHESS.EXE` (see `notes/analysis.md` "Piece graphics
  extracted") - `piece_glyphs.h`/`.c` hold it as plain data, 40x24-pixel
  1-bit-per-pixel bitmaps, one pair (black-filled, white-outline) per
  piece type, no drawing logic attached. All actual drawing goes through
  `gfx.h`, a small generic pixel interface (`gfx_fill_rect`,
  `gfx_draw_bitmap_1bpp`, `gfx_init`, `gfx_present`) with zero
  hardware-specific code in the header itself - `board_render.c` (the
  portable board-layout logic, sized for a 320x320 screen - see
  `board_render.h`) is the only caller, and never touches a framebuffer or
  driver directly. The white-piece outline needs a different ink color
  depending on which square color it sits on to stay readable (a fixed
  color can't have good contrast against both a light and a dark square) -
  `board_render.c` picks `GFX_WHITE_PIECE_DARK_INK`/`_LIGHT_INK`
  accordingly; see the `gfx_color_t` comment in `gfx.h`. Two backends exist:
  `src/gfx_ppm.c` (desktop testing - writes `chess_board.ppm` after every
  move, no display hardware needed) and `picocalc/gfx_picocalc.c` (the
  real thing - see below). 320x320 was chosen because it divides evenly
  into an 8x8 board of 40x40-pixel squares, which not coincidentally
  exactly matches the original glyphs' 40-pixel width - pieces need
  centering but no scaling.

- `picocalc/` — the PicoCalc hardware build: **the full game, confirmed
  working on real hardware, played entirely on the PicoCalc's own
  keyboard.** Separate Pico-SDK CMakeLists.txt (the desktop build above
  has nothing to do with the Pico SDK) that compiles `../src/main.c` and
  the rest of the portable core completely unchanged, plus
  `display_picocalc.c` (the `display.h` backend for this platform):

    - **Color/level selection** is a full-screen splash (`draw_splash()`),
      not an overlay on the board.
    - **Moves** are picked with a cursor: arrow keys move a highlighted
      square (yellow border) around the board; Enter on your own piece
      picks it up (green border marks the picked-up square, which stays
      lit while the cursor keeps moving); Enter on a legal destination
      plays the move; Enter back on the picked-up square puts it back
      down, unselected. An illegal Enter (empty/enemy square to pick up,
      or an illegal destination) plays a short beep
      (`audio_play_sound_blocking`, `drivers/audio.c`) instead of doing
      anything - no keyboard typing involved anywhere. ESC cancels a
      pick-up, or resigns if nothing's picked up. This is the same
      lift-and-place idea the original used with DEL/INS (see
      `notes/analysis.md`), just on arrow keys instead.
    - **`~`** (SHIFT+backtick) reboots to BOOTSEL from every single
      keyboard read in the file - splash, prompts, move input, all of it,
      via one shared helper - so reflashing never needs the physical
      BOOTSEL button. Built early and deliberately, since without it every
      iteration during development would need it (see the project memory
      on this - it's a first principle for any new PicoCalc project now,
      not just this one).

    Keyboard reading is Blair Leduc's `southbridge.c`/`sb_read_keyboard()`,
    called directly rather than through his higher-level `keyboard.c`
    wrapper (same pattern every other PicoCalc project on this machine
    uses - see `drivers/README.md`). Build (needs `PICO_SDK_PATH` and the
    ARM toolchain on `PATH`; `PICO_BOARD` is left commented out in
    `CMakeLists.txt` per usual - pass it on the command line):

      cd picocalc
      cmake -B build -G Ninja -DPICO_BOARD=pico2
      cmake --build build
      # copy build/chess-picocalc-<chip>.uf2 (`<chip>` is `RP2350` or `RP2040`, matching the board) to the PicoCalc's BOOTSEL drive

  The build also copies the `.uf2` to this top-level folder as
  `chess-picocalc-RP2350.uf2` or `chess-picocalc-RP2040.uf2` (by board), so
  both chips' builds sit side by side.

  If CMake's own compiler-check step for `picotool` or `pioasm` (both
  small C++ host tools the SDK builds from source the first time) fails
  with "Application Control policy has blocked this file" (Windows Smart
  App Control blocking a freshly-built test executable from running),
  point at already-built copies from any other PicoCalc project's build
  directory instead of letting CMake rebuild them - `pioasm`'s override
  isn't SDK-provided, `CMakeLists.txt` here adds it specifically for this:

      -Dpicotool_DIR=<path to that project's build>/_deps/picotool
      -DPIOASM_EXECUTABLE=<path to that project's build>/pioasm-install/pioasm/pioasm.exe

  The `pioasm` one must be building something with PIO for this to
  exist - `audio.c` (this project) or `audio.pio`/similar in whichever
  project you're borrowing from.

  **Windows build.** The same PicoCalc code (`picocalc/display_picocalc.c`,
  `picocalc/gfx_picocalc.c` and the shared `src/` core) also runs on Windows
  through a small SDL2 layer in `desktop/` that stands in for the PicoCalc's
  LCD, keyboard and audio drivers. From an MSYS2 UCRT64 shell with SDL2
  installed:

      cmake -S desktop -B build-windows -G Ninja
      ninja -C build-windows

  The result is `chess-picocalc-Windows.exe` in this top-level folder. SDL2 is
  linked statically, so it is a single file with no `SDL2.dll`; `~` simply
  closes the program.

  **Linux build.** The same source builds on Linux with the SDL2 development package installed
  (for example `sudo apt install libsdl2-dev`). Unlike the Windows build, SDL2 is
  **not** linked in statically: the program links `libSDL2` dynamically, and the
  build copies that library next to the executable as `libSDL2-2.0.so.0`, where
  the executable finds it through an `$ORIGIN` run-path. Keep the two files
  together.

      cmake -S desktop -B build-linux
      cmake --build build-linux

  Output: `chess-picocalc-Linux` and `libSDL2-2.0.so.0` in the top-level folder.

## Status

**Done.** The C rewrite is a complete, playable engine: legal move
generation (including castling, en passant, promotion),
check/checkmate/stalemate detection, and a working search all confirmed
by manual play. Piece movement rules, the board representation, and all
four evaluation terms (undeveloped-minor penalty, early-rook/queen-or-
uncastled-king penalty, castled bonus, and a board-control/exposure scan)
are decoded from the original and implemented - see `notes/analysis.md`
for the full decode, including a couple of the original's minor
mechanisms that were left only partially traced (not needed for a
faithful, playable rewrite): a per-piece candidate-move exclusion filter,
and a separate king-safety-specific mode of the exposure scan.

Beyond the original: a **level 0** search depth (`WHICH LOOK AHEAD LEVEL
DO YOU SELECT (0-6)?`) that plays a real but shallow search most of the
time and a uniformly random legal move the rest (`BEGINNER_RANDOM_MOVE_PERCENT`
in `chess.h`, default 35%) - gives a new player genuine chances to win
without the engine ever looking like it's deliberately losing.

The original's piece graphics have been extracted and the full game is
playable on real PicoCalc hardware (see `picocalc/` above) - board and
pieces render correctly with proper contrast on both square colors, moves
are typed on the PicoCalc's own keyboard, and `~` reliably reboots to
BOOTSEL from anywhere in the game, all confirmed on the actual device.
